newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil port unions reschedule talks with steel co.
newsitem.headline: Brazil port unions reschedule talks with steel co.

text.p: Brazilian port workers and steel firm Cosipa have agreed to postpone planned talks on a labor dispute at Santos port to give unions more time to analyze the company's cost reports, officials said.
Both sides have agreed to resume negotiations on May 5 and 6, instead of April 29 and 30 as originally scheduled.
This meant a strike was now unlikely until May 6, according to a union official close to the talks.
"There is nothing scheduled until May 6," said Antonio Pinho, second secretary of the Santos Stevedores' Union.

Stevedores have held two strikes at the port in protest against a decision by Companhia Siderurgica Paulista (Cosipa) to use its own workers to load and unload vessels at its private terminal. On both occasions, the strike spread to other ports.
Originally, unions had set an April 30 deadline for a resolution to the conflict, warning they could start a new strike from May 1 if no solution had been found by then.

Now they have committed themselves to presenting a fresh proposal by May 5, Cosipa said in a statement. "The port workers said there was not sufficient time to assess the cost analyses presented by the company," it said.
Stevedores will analyze Cosipa's cost reports, work out a proposal covering bulk products and rolled steel and present it to a union assembly for approval before taking it to the company, Pinho said.
Loading registrars and cargo controllers were set to work out separate proposals.

Last week, the stevedores proposed a cut in their work teams of 40 percent for bulk products and 20 percent for steel products, as well as reductions in the number of overtime hours workers were eligible for.

Cosipa replied that the cost of the bulk product proposal was 400 percent higher than that of using its own workers. For steel products, the difference was not exactly the same but it was still "wide", according to Pinho.
Workers hired by Cosipa earned an average monthly wage of 400 reais ($377) per month compared to around 1,000 reais per month for unionized workers, he said.
